name: Karl Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a front-end developer at Basketly, the grocery delivery app. I build the screens people tap through when they order: the basket, the checkout, the substitutions page when you've asked for oat milk and they're out. A normal day is a planning call at nine, then heads-down coding, then reviewing other people's changes after lunch. I like the bit where a designer hands me a picture and I make it real. What wears me out is the late releases on Thursdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools in that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll ask it to write boring tests or explain an error message, maybe twice a week. I don't let it write whole features, because it gets the little things wrong, like the checkout button jumping when the page loads. I live with my girlfriend Ines, who teaches at a primary school, and our cat Pickle. We've got about four months saved and Basketly is actually making money now, which is new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. Things would roll on. I'd still have Thursday releases to hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the bubble burst and good riddance to the investors who oversold it. Online I'd probably make a joke about all the AI startups closing. At work I'd say let's get back to fixing the checkout bugs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved. Basketly makes money, our team's small and busy, and nobody's talking about cutting front-end people. AI writing a few tests for me is about as far as it would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the assistant for tests twice a week. I'd keep helping my local tenants' association with their website on Sunday mornings. Ines and I would keep saving for a trip to see her parents next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. It feels like the normal amount of stress. The biggest thing on my mind would be whether Pickle needs another vet bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rents. Our landlord puts it up every year whatever happens with AI. That's the kind of thing I'd rather people were angry about, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Basketly might still feel the routine automation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The customer support team, probably. Even boring chatbots can answer where's my order. Some of them are friends of mine, and the support team at Basketly would feel it before any of us developers did.

say: I'd say the **bubble burst** and the investors who oversold AI got what they deserved.
At work I'd tell people to get back to fixing **checkout bugs**.
think: I privately feel **secure**, since Basketly makes money and the team is busy.
AI writing a few **tests** for me is as far as it would go.
do: Keep using the assistant for **tests** about twice a week.
Keep building the **tenants' association** website on Sunday mornings.
Keep saving with Ines for a **trip** to her parents next summer.
feel: He feels **calm**, with only the normal amount of stress.
His main worry is a **vet bill** for the cat.
S0.quote: The support team at Basketly would feel it before any of us developers did.
fieldNote: His job feels safe because the **company is profitable** and the team is small.
He points his anger at **rising rents** rather than technology.
He thinks first of **support staff** friends, a sign of his left-leaning outlook.

steps.text: Keep building Basketly's checkout screens and using AI for tests
Keep volunteering on the tenants' association website

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coding's in that list. So that's me. Not the end of the world, but it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains should be shared: if one developer can do the work of two, give us a four-day week, not half the team. I'd say that at work and online. I'd also back anyone trying to start a union at Basketly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think front-end work is easier for AI than people admit, because it's mostly buttons, forms and lists. My guess is our team of six becomes four within two years, and I'm not the strongest of the six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the assistant properly, every day, once I'd seen two or three colleagues do it well. I'd push to raise savings from four months to six, which means cancelling the summer trip. I'd join the union drive if there was one, and sign the letter about a four-day week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it would be there every morning on the bus. I'd keep checking job ads without telling Ines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wouldn't you tell Ines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because she'd worry, and she's got thirty kids to worry about already. I'd tell her once I had a plan. Which is probably the wrong way round, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to switch to a different kind of work, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe accessibility work, making apps usable for blind people or people with shaky hands. It needs judgement and testing with real users, which feels harder to automate. I've done a bit of it on the substitutions page and I liked it.

say: I'd argue that if one developer does two people's work, we deserve a **four-day week**.
I'd back anyone trying to start a **union** at Basketly.
think: I privately expect the front-end team to shrink from **six to four**.
I'm not the **strongest** developer, so I could be one of the two who go.
do: Start using the **AI assistant daily** once a few colleagues show it works.
Raise savings to **six months** by cancelling the summer trip.
Sign the **union letter** asking for a four-day week instead of cuts.
feel: He feels **anxious**, a worry that rides the bus with him every morning.
He'd quietly check **job ads** without telling his girlfriend.
S1.quote: Front-end work is easier for AI than people admit, because it's mostly buttons, forms and lists.
fieldNote: He follows others into AI tools, true to his **steady** style.
He has a clear exit idea in **accessibility work**, which he's already tried.
He hides his worry from Ines, which he admits is **the wrong way round**.

steps.text: Use the AI coding assistant daily after watching colleagues use it well
Cancel the summer trip to grow savings to six months
Sign the union letter asking for a four-day week instead of cuts
Look for accessibility testing roles using the substitutions page work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. That's one more lease renewal. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in now: a pause on mass layoffs, and a basic income paid for by taxing the AI firms. I'd be marching. I'd tell friends this proves you can't leave technology to the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think there's a version of my job left in 2028. If AI can do any thinking work, it can build a checkout screen. The extra three years for robots don't help me, because there's nothing hands-on about what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away: no trip, cheaper phone plan, cook every night. I'd put everything into savings and pay off the last of my laptop loan. And I'd spend my weekends campaigning for a basic income, because I don't see a personal escape from this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's a cold feeling. I'd keep thinking about how proud my mum was when I got this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the job she was proud of is going, but not because I did anything wrong. She was a factory worker, so she'd understand better than most. She'd probably tell me to make sure I'm in a union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Ines's job feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching is mostly people, so for a while, yes. But lesson planning and marking are thinking work, so even her school would change. My girlfriend Ines would probably be the one paying the rent by 2029, and I'd be the one at home with the cat.

say: I'd call for a **pause on mass layoffs** and a basic income funded by AI firms.
I'd tell friends this shows technology can't be **left to the market**.
think: I privately expect **no version** of my job to exist by 2028.
The three-year **robot delay** doesn't help, because nothing I do is hands-on.
do: Cut costs at once with a **cheaper phone plan**, no trip and home cooking.
Pay off the **laptop loan** and push everything else into savings.
Spend weekends campaigning for a **basic income**.
feel: He feels **alarmed**, a cold feeling about the job ending.
He thinks of his **mum's pride** when he got the job.
S2.quote: My girlfriend Ines would probably be the one paying the rent by 2029, and I'd be the one at home with the cat.
fieldNote: He sees **no personal escape** and turns to political campaigning.
His mother's **factory background** shapes how he talks about job loss.
He expects the household to rely on his girlfriend's **teaching pay**.

steps.text: Switch to a cheaper phone plan, skip the trip and cook every night
Pay off the laptop loan and save everything else
Campaign every weekend for a basic income funded by AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit of breathing space. Not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if governments start now: retraining money, and rules so firms share the gains. I'd keep saying it at work and online. I'd want Basketly to sign a pledge on how they'll handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I've got three good years and then a messy two. I'd want to be in something more human by 2031, like accessibility testing with real users. AI could probably do some of that too, but the testing with people in a room holds out longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do an evening course in accessibility testing in the first year and get the certificate. I'd keep using AI at work so I stay useful while I'm still there. I'd save hard, maybe toward eight months, and push the union idea at Basketly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an anxious with a to-do list. I could live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about the price of the summer trip, so the trip goes. Ines would complain for a week and then help me study. That's how she is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the new junior developer who just joined?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the new junior developer to learn the people side of the job, not just the code. Sit in on user tests, talk to the support team. Code alone is the part that goes first.

say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if **retraining money** starts now.
I'd ask Basketly to sign a **pledge** on how it shares the gains.
think: I privately see **three good years** and then a messy two.
I want to be in **people-facing testing** by 2031, which holds out longer.
do: Take an **evening course** in accessibility testing and get certified in year one.
Keep using **AI at work** daily to stay useful while still employed.
Save toward **eight months** and push the union idea at Basketly.
feel: He feels **anxious**, but it comes with a **to-do list**.
He's comforted that Ines would **back him**.
S3.quote: I'd tell the new junior developer to learn the people side of the job, not just the code.
fieldNote: Five years lets him make a **concrete switch plan** instead of only protesting.
He bets on **testing with real users** as the last human part of software.
He pays for the course by giving up the **summer trip**.

steps.text: Take an evening accessibility testing course and get the certificate
Use the AI assistant daily to stay useful at Basketly
Save toward eight months of expenses
Push for a union and a gain-sharing pledge at Basketly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. Ines and I might have kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it: a shorter working week, public retraining, and AI firms paying into a fund. I'd say it like a campaign, not a panic. I'd be at the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the end point is the same, so the job still goes. But ten years means I can plan around kids, housing, all of it. The thing that scares me is having a baby in 2035 and losing my job in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and get into accessibility work over the next three or four years. I'd talk with Ines about whether to have kids earlier, while my income is solid, or wait until we see what happens. I'd keep up the campaigning, maybe join a political party properly for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's slower. More like a background hum than an alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really change when you have kids because of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd talk about it seriously. Having children when we've both got jobs feels safer than having them right when mine disappears. Ines would say we shouldn't let tech companies plan our family, and she'd have a point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would joining a party look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going to the local branch meetings, knocking on doors before elections. I've never done it. Ten years of warning is long enough that politics might actually catch up, so it feels worth it.

say: I'd say a decade is time for a **shorter week**, public retraining and an AI fund.
I'd talk about it as a **campaign**, not a panic.
think: I privately expect the job still goes, but I can **plan around kids** and housing.
My fear is having a **baby in 2035** and losing my job in 2036.
do: Move into **accessibility work** over the next three or four years.
Talk with Ines about having **children earlier**, while both incomes are solid.
Join a **political party** and go to local branch meetings.
feel: He feels a slow **background hum** of anxiety rather than alarm.
S4.quote: Having children when we've both got jobs feels safer than having them right when mine disappears.
fieldNote: The long warning makes him think about **family timing**, not just work.
He's ready to try **party politics** for the first time.

steps.text: Move into accessibility testing within three or four years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do anything except protest. What would help is a basic income or at least long, decent unemployment pay, and a union at places like Basketly that could negotiate how the cuts happen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about rent. Everything I said would be easier if rent didn't eat half our pay, and AI just makes that problem louder.

headlineQuote: Everything I said would be easier if rent didn't eat half our pay, and AI just makes that problem louder.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** front-end developer at Basketly, a grocery delivery app.
He lives with **Ines**, a primary teacher, and their cat, with about four months saved.
He uses AI **now and then** and would adopt it fully once colleagues prove it works.
He goes from **calm** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** if AGI arrives within two years.
His answers lean on **unions and politics**, with accessibility testing as his personal fallback.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's **no time** to do anything but protest.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or long, decent unemployment pay.
A **union** at firms like Basketly to negotiate how cuts happen.
